presentation: Lead the fish 6–8 ft. Let it settle to the bottom. Two short strips as it closes, then stop — the eat comes on the stop.
notes: If one fly goes on the leader before you see anything, it is this.

presentation: Same as the pink, but you can land it closer — fish are less startled by the quieter fly.
notes: Hard white sand, high sun, fish that have seen pressure.

presentation: Lead further and strip a little more — they have to find it.
notes: Colour change is about visibility, not imitation. Low light and stirred-up water.

presentation: Rides point-up, so it can sit on the bottom without fouling. Short strips.
Short strips, longer pauses.
Land it soft and close — a foot or two in front, barely move it.
notes: The skinny-water, tailing-fish, one-shot fly. Weight is the enemy here.

presentation: Longer, slower strips than a Gotcha.
notes: The fly to show a fish that followed and refused.

presentation: Longer strips — it swims rather than hops.
notes: The upgrade when small tan flies are being refused. Fish it on the shrimp hop but stretch the strips out — a mantis swims more than it hops.

presentation: Short strips over grass, keeping it just off the bottom.
notes: Over turtle grass a tan fly vanishes; the chartreuse is a visibility decision.

presentation: Let it drop and sit. Tiny twitch, then nothing.
Put it on their nose and let it fall. Do not strip once the fish tips down.
notes: Sand bottom.

presentation: As the tan. The colour follows the bottom, not the fish.
notes: Grass and rubble bottom.

presentation: Lead, drop, stop.
Two sharp strips to kick up sand, then dead.
notes: Deeper water and moving current, where a light crab never reaches the fish.

presentation: Barely move it. A molting crab cannot run.
Cast to the edge of the blitz, never the middle. Long fast strips and do not stop.
notes: Match the bait length before you argue about colour.

presentation: Long fast strips for albies in the inlet. For redfish in the marsh, close and slower — in dirty water they hunt as much by feel as by sight.
notes: Redfish eat shrimp too, but this fly is a minnow — fish it like one. Contrast is what the colour buys you, not imitation.

presentation: Long, fast, uninterrupted.
Slower than the Clouser, and let it hang at the end.
notes: Holds a wide profile when the fish want bulk over flash.

presentation: Steady medium strips through the seam.
Pop it, then let it sit. The pause is the whole fly.
Lead the fish, let it sink to their level, slow strips. Keep stripping through the eat.
Slow. Silhouette does the work.
Lead, sink, slow strips, strip-strike hard and more than once.
Dead drift in the current, almost no strip.
notes: A handful of evenings a year, and current strength predicts it better than the moon does.
sources: https://midcurrent.com/v2/palolo-worms-and-tarpon-the-most-bizarre-hatch-in-saltwater-and-how-to-fish-it/ — accessed 2026-09-14. NOTE: Florida Keys data used as the closest available proxy; Belize-specific timing is NOT independently confirmed.

presentation: Dead drift, tight line, no indicator. Fish it as the dropper above a heavier point fly.
notes: This is the dropper in Jeff's Idaho rig.

presentation: Point fly. Its job is depth — it gets the dropper down before the drift is over.
Dead drift. The hot collar is an attention decision, not an imitation one.
In or just under the film, dead drift. This is the answer when fish are rising and refusing the dun.
Drag-free drift, upstream or down-and-across with slack. A cold drizzly afternoon is the whole point.
Flush in the film. Rises are subtle — look for the nose, not the splash.
notes: A dedicated spent-wing pattern beats this; it is a placeholder until one is added.

presentation: Dead drift on the point or the dropper.
Drag-free. A pale-bodied parachute is closer, but this will get eaten.
In the film behind a visible dry.
notes: Cripples get eaten before clean duns do.

presentation: Point fly, dead drift, tight line. Depth first.
notes: This is the fly that took the 19" cutthroat on 2026-09-12 — on point, euro rig, 3 ft seam — and the rainbow that afternoon as a dry-dropper.

presentation: Same drift; the collar buys you a look in off-colour water.
Dead drift, then let it swing and rise at the end — the pupa is rising when it gets eaten.
notes: The lift at the end of the drift is the imitation, not the fly.

presentation: Drift it, then twitch it. Splashy rises mean they want movement.
As above. Also the dry half of a dry-dropper, because it floats a nymph.
Drift and twitch.
Deep, slow, dead drift.
Suspended in the upper column, dead drift. Size down further than feels reasonable.
Dropper, dead drift.
Dead drift in slow water. It imitates a cluster, which is what they are actually eating.
Point fly, bounced along the bottom. Available all year, not just at hatch time.
Dead drift near weed and cobble.
As above. Living naturals are olive and grey.
Dead drift.
notes: Only where the naturals actually turn orange. A good example of a colour rule that does not travel between watersheds — the log will settle this one.

presentation: Point fly, deep, dead drift. Rising water after rain is the trigger.
Dead drift, deep.
Cast across, let it get down to the stones, then strip it away from the bank in sharp pulls with a pause between. The eat comes on the fall, as it turns over.
notes: The middle ground, and the one to start with. A sculpin has no flash — resist the urge to add any.

presentation: As the brown. Clear water and good light.
Silhouette does the work. Slow it down and let it hang longer at the end of the swing.
notes: Off-colour water and the edges of light — which is when the big ones hunt.

presentation: Down and across, stripped back in bursts with a pause. Loop knot so it swims.
Slower and deeper than a sculpin swing. Long soft pulls, and let it sink between them — a leech that stops is a leech that sinks.
As the black, in clearer water.
Rides point-up so it can sit on the bottom without fouling. Short strips, real pauses.
Dead drift as the dropper. The flash buys a look in broken water where the natural gets lost.
Point fly. Silhouette in thin clear water and high sun, where an olive body disappears.
